newsitem.title: THAILAND: Sam Rainsy calls for Cambodian resistance movement.
newsitem.headline: Sam Rainsy calls for Cambodian resistance movement.

text.p: Cambodian opposition leader Sam Rainsy on Tuesday called on his supporters to join a movement to resist Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who has taken control of the nation's government.

"I told my people to resist as a matter of principle...to fight against Hun Sen. We have agreed to join the resistance with the FUNCINPEC (party of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh)," he told Reuters at the Thai border town of Aranyaprathet.

He added that he met Ranariddh in France before arriving in Thailand and the message from the deposed leader was that his FUNCINPEC followers should resist Hun Sen. Ranariddh was expected to come to Thailand soon to further his cause.
Respected former finance minister Sam Rainsy heads the Khmer Nation Party (KNP), dozens of whose members have fled to Aranyaprathet from Phnom Penh fearing Hun Sen's forces.
A former member of FUNCINPEC, Sam Rainsy was expelled from the National Assembly in late 1994 after he upset powerful political figures with his campaign against corruption.

He was in Europe during Ranariddh's recent bloody ouster. At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded in Phnom Penh in fighting on July 5 and 6 between forces loyal to Hun Sen and Ranariddh. Ranariddh had left for France before the fighting began.

"I came here to look after my people. Before I came here I met with Prince Ranariddh and his message to FUNCINPEC is to resist against the dictatorship," he said. "This is not a matter of (political) parties but it's a matter of the nation."

"Democracy must fight against criminal coup d'etat. Prince Ranariddh will come to Thailand as soon as possible, as a legitimate first prime minister and as the guest of the Thai government," Rainsy said.
Sam Rainsy will leave for Thailand later today before departing to France again.

Opposition and FUNCINPEC sources said that there were about 36 frightened KNP supporters and up to 300 FUNCINPEC politicians and party supporters holed up in the outwardly calm but tense town of Poipet, on the other side of the border from Aranyaprathet.

Poipet is still under the control of about 300 royalist soldiers loyal to Ranariddh and a local administrator told Reuters that an informal ceasefire had been agreed with pro-Hun Sen forces in the area.
"We have agreed to stand still," said the administrator, but added that he was not very optimistic that the ceasefire would last for long.
A number of troops were gathered near the house of the local army commander and some people were seen playing volleyball at a court near the road side.
Cambodian traders crossed the border between the two towns as usual on Tuesday morning to buy supplies and do business on the Thai side.
Sam Rainsy accused Hun Sen of committing "an illegal, barbarian and criminal act which provoked bloodshed and plunged Cambodia into turmoil again."
He said Hun Sen had moved against the will of the people as expressed through elections organised by the United Nations in 1993. Cambodia's coalition government was formed following that poll.
"I ask Cambodian people not to lose hope in democracy, in freedom and justice. I ask all armed forces under Hun Sen's control not to obey orders to kill, harm or harass the people," he added.
"I ask soldiers to just receive orders to defect and join legitimate democratic forces who are fighting to restore the rule of law and democracy," he said.

Hun Sen has denied staging a coup against Ranariddh. He says he had to take action because Ranariddh's military commanders were bringing "illegal forces" and weapons into Phnom Penh to bolster the prince's troop strength, which Ranariddh denies.
